title: Medicaid drug money: concentration, jumps and outliers
question: Which San Francisco billers draw most of their Medicaid drug money from one or two costly drugs, saw it jump in a year, or stand far above other Bay Area billers of the same kind for the same drug?
finding: 252 San Francisco billing numbers appear in the federal Medicaid drug file with $207.4 million from 2018 to 2024 ($19.9 million in 2018, $38.8 million in 2023). 19 of them show at least one pattern (16 outside City government and the University of California): 11 with four fifths of a year's drug money on one or two high-cost drugs and well above the middle biller of its kind, 9 with a jump or a sudden start, and 5 paid at least ten times the middle Bay Area biller of its kind for a drug. Concentration by itself is ordinary in this file: in 2023 the middle Bay Area pharmacy drew 68% of its drug money from two products and the middle provider of other kinds 52%. The three largest drugs by money to San Francisco billers are drug product code 00006-3026 (no name for this code in the files on disk), $36.8 million; Infliximab (sold as Remicade; product code 57894-0030), $15.2 million; Adalimumab (sold as Humira; product code 00074-0554), $12.9 million.
how: The federal drug file gives one row per billing number, prescribing number, drug code and month. Rows whose drug code is a placeholder for a missing code (2,190 of the 227,103 rows in this extract, $45.3 million) were left out, as the federal documentation advises. Package sizes of one product were added together. For each billing number and year: the share of drug money from its two largest products, the amount per claim line for the largest, the change from the year before, and its payment for the largest product against the middle (median) of billers of the same kind in the extract, pharmacies against pharmacies. A row needs $250,000 of drug money in the year and one of: four fifths on two products with $1,000 or more per claim line and a share at least 15 points above the median biller of its kind that year; $500,000 after at least tripling or starting from under $50,000; or $250,000 for one product at ten times the median of five or more peers. Each biller is shown once, on its largest such year. Drug names are not in the drug file: a product name was taken from the federal Open Payments files, which print a name beside a drug code, and the generic name from the Medicare Part D file, which prints it beside the brand name; 52% of the money to San Francisco billers could be named this way.
limits: This says nothing about any patient, and no small count is rebuilt: the file withholds every cell under 12 claim lines or 12 people. The comparison the question deserves, against billers of the same kind across the country and across California, cannot be made here: only rows touching the project’s Bay Area provider universe were kept from the national file, so peers are other Bay Area billers. A specialty pharmacy, a hospital clinic or a practice that treats one serious illness will rightly draw most of its drug money from a few costly drugs, and a new clinic or a new drug produces a jump. The file mixes pharmacy claims with drugs given in clinics and with amounts health plans report, does not exclude denied claim lines, and counts claim lines, not quantities, so money per line is not a price; some product codes in it belong to supplies that equipment suppliers bill, not medicines. The federal documentation calls the file a transparent source rather than a cleaned one. A drug name comes from a manufacturer’s payment report for the same product code and can be wrong; codes with no name on disk are shown as codes. 2024 is preliminary.
